title: Bidirectional short-term Associations between Incidental Affect and Physical Activity: Heterogeneous Effects Beyond Individual-Specific Diurnal Patterns.
abstract: Physical activity and affective experiences play a relevant role in physical health and mental well-being and fluctuate substantially within individuals across the day. Although intensive longitudinal studies increasingly examine bidirectional within-person associations between affect and physical activity in daily life, methodological approaches for analyzing these dynamics remain underdeveloped. Further, it remains unclear to what extent short-term affect-activity associations exist beyond stable individual-specific diurnal patterns. Two intensive longitudinal datasets were analyzed (n = 68 students; n =127 general population). Momentary affective states (energetic arousal, calmness, valence) were assessed using ecological momentary assessment alongside continuously recorded step counts. Physical activity was aggregated across moving time windows ranging from 15 to 120 minutes before and after each affect assessment. Individual-specific diurnal trajectories of affect and activity were modeled using polynomial and Fourier regressions. Within-person associations were estimated before and after removing diurnal components. Across both datasets, affect-activity associations were generally small and heterogeneous across individuals. Energetic arousal showed the most consistent positive within-person associations with physical activity. Calmness exhibited weak negative associations and valence showed little systematic coupling with activity. No specific time-lag window consistently produced stronger effects. Associations between energetic arousal and physical activity persisted after adjustment for diurnal rhythms. Affect-activity relations are weak on average across individuals, yet highly person-specific with large differences in the size and direction of associations and embedded within stable daily rhythms. Future research should place greater emphasis on individualized modeling approaches that explicitly account for temporal structure and interindividual heterogeneity in within-person processes.
